speechtext: Madam Speaker, today I would like to take advantage of the provisions of Standing Order 21 to bring to the attention of the House and of the Cabinet that the situation regarding clothing imports is such that Canadian industry is being threatened. An article published in La Presse on March 17 said that imports from the Far East, including Hong Kong, Korea, Taiwan and China, were creating an increasingly threatening situation. Before the Easter holidays, Government negotiators had meetings with representatives of the countries I just mentioned and unfortunately came home empty-handed. More and more imports are coming into the country and are threatening the livelihood of the people working in the industry. I would therefore ask Cabinet to examine the situation carefully, especially considering the many letters sent by the people concerned, and more specifically, by the Canadian Institute of Clothing Manufacturers, and also since my riding is being affected by this situation, I would urge the Government to look into the possibility of applying Clause 19 of the GATT Agreement so that we could keep the quotas, ensure that there will be no increase in clothing imports, in line with agreements we had a few years ago, and protect jobs in this industry, because, Madam Speaker, the garment industry has been severely affected by the present recession. I would therefore urge Cabinet not only to look into the matter but to make a decision as soon as possible.

Madam Speaker, it has become quite clear to everyone who has any knowledge of the situation that the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has become an anachronism, and those who live under its yoke cannot be blamed for judging it to be
an instrument of colonialism wielded by a heavy-handed federal Government.
The Hon. Bud Drury in his report to the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) recommended that the Department be disbanded and that its responsibilities be conferred on either the territorial governments or other federal Departments. What could be more logical than the Department of Public Works looking after public works, or the Department of the Environment looking after environmental concerns without the unnecessary involvement of another superfluous Department?
On the Indian Affairs side a consensus is rapidly developing that the Department should be replaced by a small secretariat, the function of which would be to co-ordinate funding activities and the work of other Departments in areas where they affect aboriginal affairs.
The Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development has outlived its usefulness, and its existence should be discontinued.

Madam Speaker, today the National Anti-Poverty Organization is meeting in Ottawa and will be hosted by representatives of all Parties this evening. I was actively involved with the poor people's movement in 1971 when, following a federal anti-poverty conference, this organization was first formed. Since that time many self-help projects have come and gone, largely because of inadequate funding.
I congratulate the early pioneers, and especially those women on low incomes who have raised their children in great difficulty and are still struggling to improve conditions in their communities. I also congratulate the new NAPO which has reorganized and is showing new energy this past year.
It is not easy for poor people who live on welfare or unemployment insurance to find the energy and funds to organize and fight for their rights, and to demand changes. Yet this is absolutely essential if they are to be treated not as victims but as human beings with hope for the future.

Madam Speaker, last year, as energy critic for my Party, I went to Boston and visited the Citizens' Energy Corporation which is headed by Joseph Kennedy, eldest son of the late Senator Robert Kennedy. One of their programs was of particular interest to Canada, the HOT Program, or Home Oil Transfer Program. When home owners convert from oil to natural gas, some oil remains in their tanks in the houses or under the gardens. The Citizens' Energy Corporation pumps out the tanks, sells the oil, and donates the proceeds to the poor.
Mr. Kennedy later visited me here in Ottawa. He met with myself, the Hon. Member for Hillsborough (Mr. McMillan), as well as Joel Bell, Bill Hopper, and Peter Toews, all distinguished Canadian civil servants. Today Mr. Kennedy, brother Michael, and mother Ethel, are in Ottawa and will visit other Canadian cities to kick off a similar Canadian program with proceeds to go to a Canadian Robert F. Kennedy memorial and to the Salvation Army. If any Canadians watching or listening to the proceedings today, or Hon. Members of this House, want more information, I wish they would please contact me. Meanwhile, on behalf of all Hon. Members, may I welcome the Kennedy family to Canada and thank them for their efforts and ideas in this important area.

The Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Trudeau) is a strong man and he has used his talents to destroy much of what all of the Prime Ministers before him built. He entered the Canadian "ring" and in one fell swoop-the national energy policy-all but killed the entire gas and oil industry. Then with a left hook-the excise tax on natural gas-he crippled agriculture and the agri-food sectors. Fighting madly, he struck at the men and women who
April 13, 1983

had worked for 40 to 50 years to build a business or a farm to use it as a nest egg for retirement, by eliminating annuities and enforcing capital gains which made retirement impossible.
Still thirsting for blood, he hit at the living standard of the superannuates, the old, and even the kids, by refusing them the allowances they had been promised. With fancy footwork he let the interest rates and federal taxes rise until hundreds of businesses went bankrupt and unemployment rose to two million. With a right to the confidence of the nation, and a left to free enterprise, he sent them both reeling to the mat. Then still thirsting for money, he borrows another $19 billion, raising the debt for Canadians to pay, to more than $150 billion.
Glorying in his achievements, he darts from the "ring" and goes to the far corners of the earth leaving his Canadians divided, frustrated and depressed. Too bad this man did not use his strength to build Canada instead of destroying Canada.

subsubtopic: ACID RAIN POLLUTION-MINISTER'S MEETING WITH UNITED STATES SECRETARY OF STATE
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, my question is directed to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. The Minister and the United States Secretary of State, George Shultz, evidently agreed in Washington this week to turn the urgent problem of acid rain over to a group of Canadian and U.S. scientists to see whether they could find some common ground on which to base a bilateral accord on acid rain affecting the two countries.

As the Hon. Member knows, there is a peer group of scientists now in the United States evaluating the results of

April 13, 1983

working groups that have been dealing with acid rain, and likewise there is a scientist heading up a similar group in Canada. Both of these scientists are outside of Government service. The House resumed from Wednesday, March 30, 1983, consideration of the motion of Mr. McKinnon that Bill C-658, an Act to amend the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on External Affairs and National Defence.

Mr. Speaker, I would first of all like to thank the House for their co-operation in allowing me to stand my Bill over until this time when it could be given full discussion. This is a rather unusual Bill. I have given it a lot of thought. It has been on the Order Paper for a couple of years.
If I were to be asked what there is about this Bill to recommend it to the House, I would quote Edmund Burke, who we all know and revere as a politician of outstanding stature in the days in which he lived. Just about 200 years ago when he was running for nomination in Bristol, in taking questions at the

April 13, 1983
Canadian Forces Superannuation Act
end of his speech he was asked why he wanted to be a Member of Parliament. He replied:
I want to be a Member of Parliament so to have my share of doing good and resisting evil.
Today all Hon. Members will get a chance to have their share of doing good. I believe that "evil" is a bit hyperbolic for this situation, but there has been an injustice done in the Superannuation Act of the Canadian Forces for many years. A volunteer ex-serviceman has given me permission to use his name as an example of a case which I believe has resulted in a very serious miscarriage of natural justice. I did what I could to get this injustice corrected by writing to various Ministers, to the President of the Treasury Board, to the Minister of National Defence and to the Minister of Justice. I wrote to them on several occasions with no result. If ever I saw a case where people hid behind regulations and bureaucracy had its way, it was in the case of Lieutenant Eric Haywood of the Royal Canadian Navy.
In a letter to the then President of the Treasury Board (Mr. Johnston) on April 5, 1982, just over a year ago, I pointed out these facts, and I quote:
In 1966, then Lieutenant Eric Haywood, of the Royal Canadian Navy, was released from the Royal Canadian Navy for misconduct. He had been convicted on December 20, 1965 on five offences dealing with misappropriation or theft. He and a civilian accomplice appear to have stolen or misappropriated $606 worth of photographic supplies from the Royal Canadian Navy.
Whether he was guilty or not is a question I do not wish to quarrel with. Quoting from the same letter:
He was convicted in a civilian court and sentenced to two years on each count, sentences to run concurrently. He served something in the order of one year in jail and was then paroled.
His accomplice in this serious act was tried with him. They were tried in a civilian court for, I believe, two reasons; one, the regulations which operate in the Department of National Defence forbid them to sentence an officer to detention and, clearly, there was a likelihood of Lieutenant Haywood being sentenced to confinement in some court or other where they did not have such restrictions, such as a court martial. Second, his accomplice was a civilian. I will have quite a bit more to say about what happened to the two men who were accomplices in this act.
Mr. Haywood was released from the forces under Item 1 (b) of the table to Article 15.01 of the Queen's Regulations and Orders for the Royal Canadian Navy, which is entitled "Service Misconduct". At the time of his release the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act had the following provisions for the payment of benefits under the Act for members whose retirement was due to misconduct. Section 10 provides that a contributor who is compulsorily retired from the forces by reason of misconduct is entitled to-and in subparagraph (b) it says, and this is the critical subparagraph which my Bill amends:
-in the discretion of the Treasury Board if he has served in the Forces for ten or more years, the whole or any part specified by the Treasury Board of any annuity to which he would have been entitled under this section.
That means that the Treasury Board can decide to pay him all of his pension or any part of it. In fact, they could do away with it entirely. Under this authority, ex-Lieutenant Haywood was informed by the Treasury Board that he was to lose 50 per
cent of his pension. It should be noted that this meant an additional punishment, without a trial or any representations made on behalf of the person most involved, Mr. Haywood. The fact that the Treasury Board is not a judicial body and the fact that the judge in a court in Saanich, British Columbia deemed that a jail sentence was sufficient punishment for misappropriation with an accomplice of an amount equivalent to $606, seems not to have influenced the Treasury Board at all. It, as I have said, added its punishment of a 50 per cent loss of pension. The amount which Mr. Haywood lost because of the findings of the Treasury Board was something slightly over $50,000 a year ago. The amount is now over $55,000 which he has lost. In my letter of April 5, 1982, I said:
I am asking you to review the equity and justice of this heavy penalty imposed on top of the penalty for a first offence.
Frankly, it seemed to me that the two-year prison sentence for a first offence of stealing $606 was a fairly heavy sentence in itself. Then he had an additional $55,000 fine imposed by a non-judicial board in Ottawa. I pointed out to the then President of the Treasury Board in my letter:
I have discussed this matter by correspondence with the Minister of Justice and the Minister of National Defence. The Minister of National Defence in replying to a representation of mine, informed me on March 9 that the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act was amended in 1969 and again in 1977. He then went on to say
"Insofar as Mr. Haywood is concerned, if his case had arisen after the amendments to the Act, there would have been no change in the amount of the annuity which would have been referred to the Treasury Board for consideration. The policy of the Treasury Board appears to have changed, in that at the time of Mr. Haywood's release it seemed almost automatic that a retirement for misconduct would result in a fifty per cent reduction in the member's annuity.
Today, the Board is perhaps more compassionate and reductions in the area of twenty to twenty-five per cent are customary."
I respectively submit that Mr. Haywood has long ago paid the full price for the crime that he committed and that his pension should now be restored.
I finally received an answer to that, and I do not know what civil servant prepared it for the Minister. The then President of the Treasury Board, I assume, took responsibility for it. I would like to read part of it, which might give an idea of the kind of reply I have received from all of the Ministers on this matter. The then President of the Treasury Board said, and I quote:
The recommendation to the Treasury Board was based on a certification of the Service Pension Board, as constituted under Section 22 of the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act, that the retirement of ex-Lieutenant Haywood was compulsory because of misconduct and a concurrence that a recommendation to the Treasury Board of a 50 per cent annuity to Mr. Haywood was warranted.
This recommendation to the Treasury Board was based on the prevailing policy of the Treasury Board at that time which was that a 50 per cent reduction in the annuity payable to a member dismissed for misconduct was appropriate. You will understand, therefore, that the 50 per cent pension reduction subsequently approved by the Treasury Board in the case of Mr. Haywood was fully in accord with decisions taken during those years in numerous other similar cases of release for misconduct.
It is quite true, as the March 9, 1982 letter to you from the Office of the Minister of National Defence indicates, that in the misconduct cases which the Treasury Board has reviewed in recent years (and these have been very infrequent), the Board has approved reductions in amounts lesser than the 50 per
April 13, 1983

cent reductions approved in earlier years. This, I feel, is a reflection of more recent views concerning the extent to which pensions payable to contributors who are released from employment for reasons of misconduct should be abated.
He then goes on to make a very curious remark for a Minister of the Crown and President of the Treasury Board, and I quote:

when convicted by a service tribunal of a serious offence that warrants release under this category: when convicted by service tribunals of a number of offences indicating a course of misbehaviour that warrants release under this category: when convicted by the civil power of an offence of a serious nature related to the performance of his duties which would have warranted release under this category if convicted by a service tribunal:

Mr. Speaker, I note that the explanatory notes of Bill C-658 state:
The purpose of this Bill is to limit the extraordinary discretion of the Treasury Board under the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act to reduce substantially pensions of Canadian Forces personnel who have been discharged for misconduct, sometimes for less than major offences.
Taking it from there, I would say that contrary to what one reads in the explanatory notes, the discretion of the Treasury Board under the provisions of the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act is not extraordinary but, rather, is similar to the discretion presently exercised by Treasury Board pursuant to Regulation 41 of the Public Service Superannuation Act, which reads as follows:
Where a contributor is convicted of an indictable offence committed by him while employed in the Public Service, if the Treasury Board is of the opinion that the commission of the offence by the contributor constituted misconduct in office, any annuity or allowance payable under the Act to or in respect of the contributor shall be reduced by such amount as the Treasury Board, in its discretion, considers appropriate.
Therefore, one will see from this statement of the Public Service Superannuation Act that the individual in question is being treated just as fairly and could not expect any further fair treatment than that. Furthermore, contrary to what you read in the explanatory notes, no Canadian Forces personnel, to my knowledge, or to the knowledge of the Department so far as I know, has ever been discharged for misconduct for less than a major offence.
I submit to Your Honour that this offence was in fact a major offence. It was not only one offence, it was a series of offences. There were, in fact, five offences.

Any member who receives any one of the above-noted punishments or commits any one of the above-noted infractions has been convicted of a major offence. As such, he should not expect necessarily to receive as a right the same pension benefits as a person who was released for reasons other than misconduct. It should also be noted that although the statement was made that misconduct releases may affect those who have committed less than major offences, no attempt has been made in Bill C-658 to amend the definition of "misconduct". It may be, then, that the Hon. Member may wish to do this in the future.
Consideration must be given to the fact that, at the very worst, a member released for misconduct will receive a return of contributions under the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act and Supplementary Retirement Benefits Act pertaining to this. As well, he will receive interest thereon at the rate of 4 per cent compounded annually.
Any attempt to make the proper legislation retroactive to January 1, 1946, is unacceptable for two basic reasons. I think the Hon. Member has noted his own error in this, although I do not believe he gave the appropriate answer.
First, Bill C-658 is attempting to amend the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act, and as the Act only came into effect in 1959, one cannot amend an Act retroactively to a point in time when the Act did not exist. The Hon. Member did point that out.
Second, any amendment in the manner proposed would be inequitable, as some ex-members would have already chosen a return of contributions rather than elected for reduced annuities, while other members in receipt of a reduced annuity would now be deceased. All members knew, or should have known, both the legal implication of their criminal activities and also the possible pension implications. I suppose we would say that there is a presumption of knowledge as far as the law is concerned. One is presumed to know. I think that applies to all of our laws. One is presumed to know the nature and consequences of one's act, and one is presumed to know the law; yet individuals sometimes choose to commit offences. As such, they should not expect special consideration at this late stage.
I further note from the explanatory notes:

The new scheme would basically limit Treasury Board's power to intervene by deeming the total period of pensionable service to expire at the time of the commission of an offence and allowing that period to be reduced by a maximum of 12 months for the purposes of calculating the annuity payable.

This, in fact, is a more liberal benefit than that which is recommended in Bill C-658. Moreover, the existing Section provides some discretion which might apply in exceptional circumstances. I do not really know whether special circumstances can be shown in this case, but perhaps they can. It may be that the longer period of service in itself, some 26 years, should be taken into account. It is a long period to find that one would have his or her pension reduced by one-half.
As the law presently stands, there is no reason why this decision would not stand in the absence of any other evidence to the contrary. Since the Hon. Member is obviously referring to the Haywood case, I can mention it. I assume that was the case he was referring to when preparing his Private Member's Bill. The facts of the case are rather interesting and I suggest they should be put on the record. In October of 1965, this exmember was convicted by the civil authorities at Victoria, British Columbia, on each of five charges of fraud and theft under the Criminal Code of Canada. He was sentenced to the term of two years' imprisonment on each count, such sentences to run concurrently. In other words, he did not serve ten years, two years for each conviction, but the five two-year terms were to run concurrently. The charges arose out of the misuse of photographic equipment which was the property of the Royal Canadian Navy Photographic Establishment at Esquimalt, British Columbia.
As a result of his conviction the ex-member was released from the Royal Canadian Navy on May 31, 1966, under Item 1(b) of the table to Article 15.01 of the Queen's Regulations and Orders for the Royal Canadian Navy entitled "Service Misconduct".
At the time of his release the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act had the following provisions for the payment of benefits under the Act for members whose retirement was due to misconduct. I believe it is noteworthy that these Sections of the Act are somewhat different from what they presently are. In fact, the Hon. Member for Victoria alluded to them in part.
Section 10(5) indicates that a contributor who is compulsorily retired from the Armed Forces by reason of misconduct is entitled to:

It goes on to indicate some other Sections as well. However, I think we should take into account that there is the presumption of knowledge of the law although it may not have in fact been known by the perpetrator of the crime. By the same token, I have never yet met anyone who was charged with a criminal offence who expected to be caught. In a meeting held on August 15, 1966, the Service Pension Board certified that it had determined that the reason for the retirement of the ex-member was compulsory because of his misconduct. At the same time the Board concurred that, in accordance with the provisions of a policy guide on discretionary awards, the member's retirement warranted a recommendation to the Treasury Board of a reduced annuity pursuant to Section 10(5)(b), Subsection 2, of the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act. The so-called policy guide was one adopted by the then Associate Minister of National Defence on discretionary authority of the Treasury Board to approve certain benefits under the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act.
On September 1, 1966 the Treasury Board approved an annuity reduced by 50 per cent, as has been pointed out. I am sure that at the time this was brought forward the amount involved was considered to be rather nominal in nature. The amount is as large as it is today due to the numbers of years that have passed since this order was made.
Apparently the ex-member has applied to the Service Pension Board on numerous occasions since September, 1966 for a review of his case. On every occasion the Board members were unanimous in their opinion that the Board ruling of August, 1966 and the subsequent award by the Treasury Board should not be disturbed. I think it is important to note that they were unanimous on every occasion that he took this matter before the Board.
The ex-member was subsequently granted a pardon by the Governor in Council in accordance with the provisions of the Criminal Records Act. As a result of this pardon, the Service Pension Board was faced with the problem of whether the pardon vacated the disability placed on the ex-member's annuity and whether it meant that the annuity should be restored to its full amount. It should be appreciated that when one applies for a pardon it only pertains to the conviction that was lodged and not to any of the other consequences following therefrom.
The matter was referred to the Department of Justice which advised that the pardon granted under the Criminal Records Act did not affect in any way the decision of the Treasury Board to specify that the ex-member was entitled to 50 per cent of the total annuity that could be awarded to him under the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act.
When the ex-member was advised that the Service Pension Board decided that no change in the Treasury Board ruling with respect to his annuity was indicated as a result of the opinion from the Department of Justice, he appealed directly to the Treasury Board itself. After a complete review of all the material available on his case, the chief of the Treasury Board pension group advised the ex-member that as a result of the opinion expressed by the Department of Justice she could not accede to his request for a review of his entitlement under the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act.
In order for a decision to be reversed in this matter, the exmember would have to submit new evidence to the Service Pension Board concerning the original offence which led to his dismissal. As well, the nature of that evidence would have to be such that the Board could reasonably conclude that the reason for his release was not in fact misconduct as defined in the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act. I would suggest that this is indeed a very heavy onus upon this ex-serviceman. Obviously if there was any evidence it should have been presented at the time of his trial, and if there was any evidence available that was not presented, he may have had an appeal at that time.
In any event, that was not the case. In the absence of his ability to oblige this obviously extensive onus placed upon him, nothing further could be done. While the amount of the reduction may seem harsh by present day standards, we must accept the fact that penalties were more severe in cases of misconduct release at the time of the Treasury Board decision. It should be noted that in misconduct cases which the Treasury Board has reviewed in recent years, which have been very infrequent, the Board has approved reductions in amounts lesser than the 50 per cent reduction approved in earlier years. Obviously times have changed since this happened some 17 years ago. Perhaps there would be a great difference today and the amount would be less, but anyone who has received a sentence years ago cannot expect to have it reversed years later and have a lesser sentence meted out by the courts or the tribunal.
Of course, this is a reflection of the more recent views concerning the extent to which pensions payable to contributors who are released from employment for reasons of misconduct should be abated. I note that there has been a tremendous amount of correspondence in regard to this matter from various Departments, including the Department of National Defence and the Treasury Board, with the Hon. Member for Victoria.
I would point out to him that this is not as though it was a case of a first offence, as he has alleged. It is actually a situation in which there are five offences. Furthermore, they are not five offences where one conviction results; it is a case of five offences and five convictions. It is a case where there was an individual sentence of two years on each of the convictions. There is no doubt that the sentence which was meted out was a proper one for the court or the tribunal to consider at that time. The penalty was in fact served.

Mr. Speaker, I have a few words to say on Bill C-658 which is sponsored by the Hon. Member for Victoria (Mr. McKinnon). This Bill seeks to amend the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act.
My good friend, the Hon. Member for Etobicoke-Lakeshore (Mr. Robinson), has done quite a good job of informing the House of some of the circumstances from which this Bill flows. There is no doubt the Hon. Member for Victoria is well motivated, as he usually is. I appreciate full well what he is attempting to do. I just want to say to him in all candour that I do not think he can do what his Bill asks, not because he does not have a majority in this House to support his Bill in the particular issue, but because in principle it would be wrong for this kind of Bill to pass. If we reduce this legislature, this House of Commons, to a place where we have to tailor a Bill, an act of Parliament, to the particular circumstance of every individual in this country, the permutations are large in number. I did not say a Bill for every individual in this country. That would require only about 24 million Bills. I said an
Canadian Forces Superannuation Act
Act for every circumstance in the life of every person in this nation. You are talking hypothetically of billions of permutations.
What this House is intended to do is something different. It is not intended to write a rule book to address every conceivable circumstance in the country. It is intended, among other things, I submit, Mr. Speaker, to provide protection for people as a whole in this country, to provide opportunities for them, and to provide constraints within which they must operate.
The gentleman who is the focal point of this piece of proposed legislation knew full well the constraints in which he was expected to operate. It is my understanding, and the information which my friend from Etobicoke-Lakeshore read into the record has not been contradicted, that the gentleman concerned elected, as is his prerogative, to operate outside those constraints. For that there were penalties.
I do not believe the time of the Hon. Member for Victoria, my time or your time, Mr. Speaker, would be well served if we were asked in effect to change the rules after the fact. To present a case of someone who operated outside certain legislative constraints who would now like to have the constraints tailored to suit his circumstances; is there anybody in this country who believes that is a proper role for this Parliament to undertake? I do not, Mr. Speaker. I believe, knowing the gentleman from Victoria as I do-not well, but I believe I know him well enough-I do not believe he sees that as a role for this particular Parliament.
I say to him and to Parliament that I believe he finds himself in a fairly unenviable position. He has been supplicated by an individual who clearly has a very real problem, a problem which imposes upon him many financial implications. If a sweep of the pen could make the financial situation of that gentleman easier, 1 am sure in principle no one here would be against it. I am not against it. But I tell you what I am against, Mr. Speaker. I am against setting a precedent which would know no end. This case has floodgate implications. If after the fact you were to broaden the constraints which were well understood, legislated in good faith and abided by almost everyone, what would happen if you were told there was one individual who chose not to abide by them? I have said already that it is his prerogative to make that kind of election. But I learned a long time ago, and I believe everyone in this House has learned likewise, that for every act there is a consequence; and for every action there is a reaction. Everything you do and everything you say triggers a set of events. Simply put, I believe-no pun intended-that this man has had his day in court.
From what I have read, I believe he has been treated fairly. I believe it is time to let sleeping dogs lie. I say to my friend from Victoria, let us put this one to bed. Give the Hon. Member an "A" for effort. He has tried, and he has aired the case. He has aired it in a proper fashion. He has done the right thing by raising the case. The Hon. Member must know there is no way that this initiative can succeed. It cannot succeed because of the awesome precedent it has the potential of setting.

Much has been made of the pardon obtained in this case. As I understand the Statute under which this pardon was obtained, such pardons are intended to facilitate the future activities of those pardoned, not to undo the past. The pardon does not say that we will undo the past. It does not say that this never happened. It does not say that the finding of the court was in error. Do not let it be suggested for a moment that the provision of a pardon is tantamount to suggesting that the court was in error in the first place. We all know that was not the reason for the pardon or the spirit within which the provision of pardons was legislated. Pardons are there to facilitate the future activities of individuals who have need of such.
The discretionary power vested in Treasury Board in this particular type of case is there for very good reason. We often hear in a country as large and as diverse as ours, trying to address many problems, that our legislation could run into the danger of lacking some compassion and flexibility. We have a number of mechanisms for addressing the problem of potential inflexibility. We do it by setting out broad parameters in law or in legislation which we put through the House. Then we allow certain discretionary powers to flow from that broad legislation. If we were to make the mistake of locking into law or statute every single possible occurrence and were to try to anticipate every wrinkle which could flow from a statute and then incorporate in law a provision to accommodate that wrinkle, of course we would be here all the time, and I do not think we would be serving the country very well.
Thus we do something else instead. We vest certain discretionary powers. Who are these people in Treasury Board? Are they people who have an axe to grind with an individual, probably? Are they people who are on a witch hunt, maybe? Are they people who get their jollies out of adversely affecting the financial situation of someone thousands of miles away? I do not believe that; I just do not believe that. I believe those people who made that decision and exercised that discretionary power properly vested in law did so fairly, with compassion and at the same time dispassionately, without grinding any axes toward any particular individual. It is not that Mr. Speaker has to take my word for it because I understand the Department of Justice has indicated exactly what I just said. Justice has said that Treasury Board acted honourably and properly in this particular case.
We cannot have our cake and eat it too. We cannot in one debate parade the Department of Justice as an instrument of Government whose advice is listened to and in this debate forget the respect we have for that instrument and say that they should have no discretion, that we should cross every "t" and dot every "i".
Let us be clear about what we are talking. We have a case which has had the benefit of the full process-the judicial, the executive and the governmental process. The case has been
well aired, well heard and well adjudicated. I find no dissent. I find no minority reports from Treasury Board on the issue. I find no evidence that there were suspicious circumstances, and by that I mean circumstances which would tend to suggest that the individual was being scapegoated in some particular fashion. I find no evidence of any of this whatsoever.
Indeed, if we were to line up the forces on either side of the argument, we would find the Department of Justice, whose opinion I respect, on one side; we would find Treasury Board on the same side; and we would find Parliament on this side because it passed the Canadian Forces Superannuation Act in the first place. We would find them all on this particular side, save one or two individuals.
If I were in the gentleman's situation, I would be on the same side as he. Understandably we find the person whose pension has been adversely affected on the other side of the issue, and somewhat understandably the Hon. Member for Victoria is on that particular side of the issue. He is on that side for another reason, but an equally good one. Obviously he does not stand to gain financially in any way, but as a Member of Parliament he wants to be sure that he does the right thing. I think he is doing the right thing. If I were in his situation, I would be doing the same kind of thing. I would be airing this to the fullest extent. I would be ensuring that no stone was left unturned. I would have this matter fully aired on behalf of the gentleman concerned. But I suggest that these are the only two individuals, both for good reason, who are on the other side of the argument.
It is significant that of all speakers who participated this afternoon it is only the Hon. Member for Victoria who has spoken from his side. Maybe he wants to take a few minutes of the time of the House to find if there is someone else who will support the case he puts. I am not referring to his right to put that case. I support his right to put it, but I do not believe, in all candour, that he has a supportable case. That may well be the reason it is he alone who stands in the House and advocates his position. I say he does it because he has to. I do not say that in any pejorative sense. I defend his right to do what he is doing today, but having done it, I think he should put the issue to rest.
The case has been well aired. I believe that the right decisions have been made and that we would commit a travesty this afternoon if we took any steps which would undermine the decisions made in this case.
Hear, hear!

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. It will be very short. I am sure the last Member who spoke would not want to mislead the country unwittingly. The New Democratic Party supported my motion and my Bill.

I was unaware of that. I thank the Hon. Member for bringing it to my attention and to the attention of the House.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING JOB OPPORTUNITIES FOR CERTAIN UNILINGUAL PUBLIC SERVICE EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
that Bill C-666, an Act to amend the Official Languages Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture.
He said: Mr. Speaker, may I refer to the explanatory note on this Bill to amend the Official Languages Act. The purpose of this Bill is three-fold. It would amend and enshrine in legislation paragraph 7 of the House of Commons Resolution of June 6, 1973, on official languages and certain principles respecting employment in the Public Service of Canada and to extend its application to Crown corporations, the Armed Forces, and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police.
The amendment to paragraph 7 would provide that any person employed in the above-stated categories as of the Royal Assent of the Official Languages Act in 1969 would not be subject to the Act's provisions or the interpretations of the provisions. It would also ensure that private companies applying for or under contracts or subject to grants from the federal Government would not be forced to comply with provisions or interpretations of the provisions of the Official Languages Act which the Secretary of State (Mr. Joyal) is proposing in his Bill C-398.
This particular Bill would impose Sections of the Official Languages Act on the private sector, and for non-compliance they would receive jail sentences and fines.
The bill to amend the Official Languages Act would give greater credibility to the notion of the "merit principle" as a basis for hiring and promotion in the civil service by reinforcing the vested rights of a generation of civil servants who may be fully qualified for designated positions but who may not have had the aptitude to learn the French language and thus have been denied promotion.
I would point out that there has never been any all-Party approval for any of the items I have just mentioned. Any time this issue was raised in the House or elsewhere, we would get the standard answer from the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) or Members of his Cabinet that this has all-Party approval. I want to assure the House that there has never been any allParty approval to dead end fully qualified, English-speaking Canadians.
Official Languages Act
Another matter that is causing considerable concern across the country is a recent speech made by the Hon. Serge Joyal, the Secretary of State for Canada, where in his speech he pointed out that he is going to turn Canada into a French state. I have no recollection of any discussion in the House of a proposal to turn Canada into a French state. In this speech that the Minister made in Halifax, he also stated that he is going to make Canada a French country, both inside and outside Quebec. I do not know what that means and how that is going to affect English-speaking Canadians, but the plan to turn Canada into a French state is something that the Government should be explaining to the Canadian people.
In the Secretary of State's recent speech in Halifax, he stated:
My role as Secretary of State is first and foremost to ensure that my French compatriots in Canada feel with deep conviction, as 1 do, that this is their country and that it reflects their image.
I do not think we can argue with that. He goes on to state:
-the ambition of making Canada a French country both inside and outside Quebec.
The Minister certainly puts his cards on the table and tells us exactly what his aspirations are. He continued:
Because everything we undertake and everything we are doing is to make Canada a French state.
I imagine when he says "we" he is referring to the present Liberal Government.
Mr. Yalden, the Commissioner of the official languages program, has stated that it is time the Liberal Government told the country what its official languages program is all about; but its reluctance to do that is what is causing so much division and confusion in the country. I have acted in accordance with this statement of Mr. Yalden's by calling for debate in Parliament on this issue. Many of the points that the Liberals should be acting upon are described in my Official Languages Bill.
I would like to refer to a recent questionnaire that I distributed in my riding asking if my constituents would like to have a full and open parliamentary debate on whether they support the Liberal Government's policies of making Canada a fully bilingual country. I received the highest return on this questionnaire that I have ever received over the past 10 years. Ninety-seven per cent voted for having a full-scale parliamentary debate so the present Government could explain its bilingual policies to the Canadian people.
This questionnaire was also distributed widely throughout Ontario and I received approximately 1,200 of these questionnaires back. Ninety-nine point seven per cent of respondents stated yes, they wanted a parliamentary debate on the discriminatory elements of the Government's bilingual policies. You can see the concerns that we have across the country, Mr. Speaker.
Here are some points of discussion that we could have in regard to abuses of the Official Languages Act. Parliamentary

April 13, 1983
Official Languages Act
legal opinion is that the Official Languages Act is very loosely worded and is open to broad interpretation. If a Minister instructs his Department to implement the Official Languages Act without filling in the details and thus without acting responsibly, then the discretionary powers of the officials charged with the duty are practically limitless. This results in the abuses of the original intent of the Act and opens the doors to broad exaggerations of the original policy. Examples of this are Franco-banks, quotas, hiring teams, and the dead ending of qualified Anglophones.
Here are a few examples of how unilingual English Canadians are being discriminated against as a result of the hiring and promotion practices of the present Government. These examples are evidence of the necessity for laws to protect English-speaking Canadians.
A former Member of a Government agency described by superiors as a "very loyal and dedicated" employee is threatening to go to court and sue for damages because of bilingual policies which prevent her from regaining her job. She has been denied re-employment only because she does not have a "desired knowledge of the French language". The following is an excerpt from her letter. I would also like to point out that this individual has two diplomas from two schools received upon learning and passing a test in the French language. This is what the individual has stated:
As an English speaking citizen of Canada, I find this unacceptable as 1 have proven that 1 am not adverse to learning the second official language. What I cannot understand is why any federal agency or Government Department for that matter is denying a Canadian citizen employment solely on the fact he or she cannot speak one of the second official languages. In the past the foundation of hiring and promotion was based on merit. Has this long established, fair and used standard of hiring the best suited person for the position been changed to one of linguistic qualifications only?
Unfortunately that is what is happening in Canada.
Furthermore, why are they not taking my qualifications and experience into consideration?
The staffing and personnel officer had written the following in regard to this individual in answer to this person's question regarding re-employment:
We would like to assure you that the reason not to process your application for re-engagement is based solely on a matter of bilingualism.
There has never been any all-Party approval for any such thing. The individual's appraisal reads as follows:
This young member impressed me quite favourably and I would have to say that the agency is losing a very loyal and dedicated employee.
The recommendation given at the time of the appraisal was that favourable consideration be given to an application for a position should she seek employment at some future time. Another staffing and personnel officer had made these comments: "She is reported as a good employee and should be given serious consideration should she reapply in the future."
This individual has all the qualifications but they will not rehire her because she cannot pass a certain level language proficiency test. A third authority in the Department said: "I agree with the recommendation to hire this person", but they
would not hire her because she could not pass the severe language training test.
I should like to read now from an RCMP directive. It is now under investigation by the Human Rights Commission which I hope will hand down a decision very shortly. It reads in part as follows:
Since there is still an urgent need to recruit first official language French bilingual applicants, I urge you all, Members and public servants to make a special effort towards the force's bilingual recruiting program. While normal recruiting programs such as advertising campaigns through the news media, participation in career days, high school visitation et cetera, have brought about good results, I firmly believe more can be done on an individual "word of mouth" basis. More specifically, people you come in contact with such as neighbours, acquaintances and relatives provide an excellent base to stimulate our recruiting efforts. Our employees are therefore encouraged to alert any person they may come in contact with whom they feel has the potential to become a member of the force.
What all this means is that they are recruiting one nationality for jobs in the RCMP and that fully-qualified, Englishspeaking members of the RCMP who do not have the aptitude to learn the French language and cannot pass the severe proficiency test are being denied promotion. That is ridiculous in a paramilitary organization. What we want is the most qualified police officers going to the most senior positions, but that is being disregarded.
I should like to quote now from a letter issued by the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs regarding hiring, recruitment and promotion of Francophones. The letter points out that this is being done to the exclusion of any other Canadian nationality. This is discrimination; it is special, preferential treatment for one nationality for hiring. The correspondence reads in part as follows:
There are many rumours circulating in the office that the hiring team presently seeking examiners has been instructed to limit their search to Francophones and particularly to unilingual Francophones. It has been further alleged that academically-qualified Anglophones have been rejected.
There has never been any discussion of any kind of policy like this and there has not been all-Party approval for any kind of discriminatory hiring and promotional practice. It is time that this matter was fully and completely debated in this House. The letter continues:
The possibility that these rumours could be true appears to be supported by the apparent attempt to keep bilingual positions open for those Francophones being hired rather than offering these positions to bilingual examiners presently in unilingual English positions. Such rumours have considerable impact on morale in the office and invite discredit. Such practices are also contrary to the "merit principle".
The purpose of my Bill is to make paragraph 7 law. It would enshrine the merit system in law so that the Government could not implement this kind of discriminatory hiring and promotional practice. The letter continues:
It is time that such rumours were squelched. Of the many ways in which you could do this, we would like to suggest that you assure all the staff of the office that these rumours are unfounded and that you support them by publication of the criteria being used for hiring.
English-speaking public servants have, since the passage of the Official Languages Act, consistently been losing ground in their attempts to be treated equally with their French-speaking counterparts. Another example is the case of an air traffic
April 13, 1983

controller who was going to lose his job about five years ago because he did not have the aptitude to learn the French language. Ele had to spend five years in the courts to try and save his job and finally had to go to the Supreme Court before there was a ruling that the Government could not dismiss him because he could not learn the French language. The Supreme Court ruled on a section of the 1973 language resolution. My Bill proposes that paragraph 7 be made law. Canadian citizens would then not have to spend five years in the courts in an effort to save their jobs because they do not have the aptitude to learn the French language.
I should like to quote a portion of a memorandum which was issued following an energy sector management meeting of the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources. It reads as follows:
From now on, all French-speaking candidates should be considered exceptional and, therefore, subject to clear-track hiring. Managers should feel free to hire Francophones without interference.
Why is only one nationality being declared exceptional, Mr. Speaker? I do not recall any discussions like that taking place in the debates of 1969 or 1973. There has never been all-Party approval to declare one nationality exceptional over other nationalities in this country.
An Armed Forces order states as follows:
Government policy dictates that departments and agencies are to ensure that an equitable participation of both official language groups is achieved. With the intent of meeting this requirement the CF attempts to maintain an Anglophone/Francophone cultural balance, relative to the NRG ratio, where possible, in each rank in each officer classification. To reach this balance, adjustments may be made to the merit list sequence in order to satisfy NRG requirements.
This points out that that merit is not always used for promotion in the Armed Forces. The order continues as follows:
Where such an adjustment has been made, the promotion of an officer who should have been promoted because of that adjustment, will be "protected". If his supervising officers' recommendations for promotion and his medical status have not changed, an officer whose promotion has been protected will be promoted when a new promotion quota is authorized for his rank and officer classification.
It could take years for that particular Anglophone to catch up, Mr. Speaker. He would lose out under an arrangement like this. This particular promotional practice has been under investigation by the Canadian Human Rights Commission since June, 1980. I hope it will hand down a decision in the near future.
One of the most ridiculous things I have come across is that today the Government is declaring that operators of English word processors be bilingual. For example, a fully qualified word processor operator cannot gain employment in the civil service because she is not bilingual even though the position she applied for is to use an English word processor. This occurred at the Export Development Corporation and is another example of discrimination. I would certainly like the Government to explain why an individual needs a knowledge of the French language in order to operate an English word processing machine. This person has a degree and all the
Official Languages Act
qualifications; she applied for the job to operate this word processing machine but was turned down.
I hope the Government will agree to make paragraph 7 law so that we can stop this type of discrimination in the Armed Forces, the RCMP and the federal civil service.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING JOB OPPORTUNITIES FOR CERTAIN UNILINGUAL PUBLIC SERVICE EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on December 15, 1982, the Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie) moved for first reading of Bill C-666, to amend the Official Fanguages Act. I am rather surprised to hear him talk about discrimination in connection with official languages and members of the RCMP who must have a knowledge of both official languages for their work. I think it is deplorable that today, in 1983, fourteen years after the Official Fanguages Act was passed, this should be a subject for debate. I think it shows crass ignorance of Canadian reality, Mr. Speaker.
However, before proceeding with a clause-by-clause examination of the proposals being made by the Member for Win-nipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie), I would like to make a few general comments which, I trust, will provide some insight into the real nature of the amendments he is proposing to the Official Languages Act and consequently help to judge the relevance of his proposal.
Clause 1 of the Bill provides that the Official Languages Act is amended by inserting, immediately after Section 35, a number of new sections.
I wondered why the Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine decided to have the amendments inserted after Section 35, and why he used the same number, followed by decimals .1, .2, .3 and .4, and kept number 40 for the clause on contracts and grants.
If we look at Section 35 of the present Official Languages Act, we see that it provides that the Governor in Council may make such regulations as he deems necessary to effect compliance with the Official Languages Act in the conduct of the affairs of the Government of Canada and departments and agencies of the Government of Canada. Now, the purpose of Section 35 is to avoid encumbering the Act with measures that are regulatory and administrative instead of straightforward legislation. If we look at the proposals contained in this Bill, we see that some of them are purely administrative, while others have already been laid down either in legislation or in separate regulations. I think this is a very important point that we should bear in mind throughout the debate this afternoon.
I would also like to point out, Mr. Speaker, that the series of amendments comprised under Clause 1 of the Bill are presented under the general heading "Language of Work". I am not sure whether the Hon. Member means to restrict the scope of his recommendations to the language of work, since the

April 13, 1983
Official Languages Act
Government has already provided that as a general rule, public servants, subject to the provisions of the Official Languages Act relating to service to the public, should be able to carry out their duties within the Government of Canada in the official language of their choice. If such were the case, this Bill would be even less commendable-if that were possible- because, on one hand, its long term effect would be to isolate such closely related goals as service to the public, equitable participation and working language, and on the other hand, it would legislate on aspects of the policy which do not exclusively relate to the working language as a goal. Indeed, the linguistic identification of jobs, the urgent and non-urgent staffing, as well as the exemptions apply to all civil servants, be they assigned to serve the public or to internal management or both at the same time, as it does happen fairly frequently.
In that respect, the Bill is far from being clear and, in my opinion, it reflects the sponsor's lack of familiarity with the Government's official languages policy. In any event, Mr. Speaker, we should rejoice that nearly ten years after the passage of the parliamentary resolution of 1973 by the House, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine is proposing today that we incorporate in the Official Languages Act new sections which, he states, are the extension of paragraph 7 of the resolution. That seems to me to be all the more relevant as the Hon. Member, I was told, did vote against the resolution in 1973. It does not come as a surprise to me.
Before rejoicing too hastily, however, we ought to ask ourselves whether we would be justified to take this step. Does the Bill stem from the Hon. Member's constructive intellectual progress with respect to the official languages program? Is it the omen of a better understanding of the Government's goals in the field of the official languages, an understanding based on a close, though belated, scrutiny of the Canadian reality in all its complexity?
When I read what the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine is advocating in his Bill, I detect, beyond its obvious banality, rather than an evolution of his thinking patterned, as we would have wished, after the evolution of the thinking of the great majority of Canadians, but indeed an almost obsessional relentlessness to stop any progress when it comes to the official languages of Canada.
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member claims that this Bill is an extension of paragraph 7 of the 1973 parliamentary resolution. Not only is he straying away from it, as I will demonstrate in a few moments, but worse still he does not respect the letter and especially the spirit of the resolution in his Bill which is supposed to be a step forward in achieving the Government's goals with respect to the official languages.
Were we to endorse this Bill, we would collectively accept to backtrack, and I am convinced that the House and most Canadians would never agree to that. Since 1969, we have had 14 years of linguistic reform, 14 years of unmistakable
progress, 14 years of cooperation on the part of civil servants, which have made it possible to respect everyone's rights and provide our country with a Public Service which is increasingly qualified to serve Canadians in the official language of their choice. After so many years of sustained efforts, strategic withdrawals would be untimely, no matter how the Hon. Member is seeking our support.
Let us now consider this Bill clause by clause. Clause 35.1 provides that the chief executive officer of each public sector employee shall identify those positions under his direction that require:
(a)	the use of both the English and French languages;
(b)	the use of the English language;
(c)	the use of the French language;
(d)	the use of either the English or the French language.
The addition of clause 35.1 to the Official Languages Act does not alter in any way the official languages policy since the procedure for the identification of bilingual positions has been enforced in the Public Service of Canada since 1973 as well as those for the identification of positions where French or English are essential and those where either French or English may be used.
Indeed, since 1973, the identification of language requirements for positions is done within the Public Service of Canada on a continuous basis as soon as a new position is created or becomes vacant thus enabling managers to review constantly the language requirements of positions for which they are responsible to make sure that such identification is done in a rational way and on the basis of the clients' actual needs and/or according to their responsibilities at the working language level in matters of internal management.
At the very beginning of the linguistic reform, the fact that the Public Service was considered as being a bilingual institution had an effect on the identification of linguistic requirements of positions. With the 1977 policy revision which came as a result of a constant follow-up, according to which a position is only identified as bilingual if there is a need to provide effective services to the public or to employees, this situation was corrected and the linguistic requirements of the positions were based on the specific requirements of the job to determine the use of either language in carrying out the duties of a given position.
The Government is not trying to promote individual bilingualism but wants to make sure that bilingual positions are only created when needed so that uniligual individuals from both official linguistic groups may operate as much as possible in their first official language.
Indeed, when we look at the statistics, Mr. Speaker, we realize that the three types of unilingual jobs account for 73.6 per cent of all civil servants or 165,890 employees using one official language only as against 26.4 per cent or 59,432 employees using both official languages in bilingual positions.
April 13, 1983

This means that within the functionally bilingual federal institutions, there are 165,890 employees operating in unilingual positions, of which 135,140 or 81.5 per cent are in jobs that are identified as exclusively English, 16,870 or 10.1 per cent in jobs identified as exclusively French and 13,880 or 8.4 per cent in jobs identified as either French or English.
As may be seen, without this proposal having ever been included in the Official Languages Act, the Government has already acted on this the way the program is being implemented. So there is nothing new in the Hon. Member's proposal. Why must we oppose the addition of clause 35.1 to the Official Languages Act? For the simple reason, Mr. Speaker, that it seems unwise to include in a statute provisions of an administrative nature. As I said, under section 35 of the Official Languages Act, the Governor in Council may make such regulations as may be needed from time to time, without the Act itself having to be brought back before Parliament. The administrative procedure for the formal linguistic identification of jobs that is used throughout the departments, Government agencies considered as departments and Crown Corporations under Schedule B of the Financial Administration Act, is followed to a lesser degree, according to the type of agency and the terms of reference of the Crown Corporations listed under Schedules C and D and others that are not.
While Crown Corporations are subject to the Official Languages Act and relevant Government policies, the program may be and is indeed implemented differently as in departments. Especially so, Mr. Speaker, when it comes to the identification of jobs as being bilingual or otherwise. For various reasons, some corporations have decided on a system in which the number of bilingual people required is determined, without formally identifying any of the positions involved as being bilingual. In some cases, such a format has its merits. This kind of flexibility would be lost were Bill C-666 to pass. By way of legislation this would convey to the official languages policies a kind of rigidity that was never intended by Parliament and from which the program has been spared up till now.
These measures, Mr. Speaker are purely administrative in nature. If they were to become compulsory, the official languages policy would be deprived of all the flexibility needed to meet the various conditions it is constantly faced with.
Earlier the Hon. Member referred to some kind of discrimination where a man had to fight for five years so as to keep the job they wanted to take away from him because he could not pass a language proficiency test under the Official Languages Act-just about anything is possible in this day and age-but I suggest he went a bit too far when he accused the Government of discriminatory hiring and promotion practices. He claimed that it was unfair because this man simply lacked the aptitude to learn French and that it was discriminatory to
Official Languages Act
make the learning of French a condition for hiring. I find this hard to believe in 1983, when Francophones are learning and being exposed to English, when Federal Civil Servants have easy access to all sorts of learning facilities, when a bilingual bonus is paid to all those who must speak both languages in the performance of their duties. Mr. Speaker, I think that situations such as this in 1983 ... The Hon. Member referred to cases where individuals had to spend 5 years in court, but when he started to talk about discrimination, Mr. Speaker, as a Francophone, I just could not buy that.
Under Section 35.2, the Hon. Member dealt in three paragraphs with hiring practices for bilingual, English-essential or French-essential positions.
The first paragraph states that knowledge of the English and French languages shall be included among the elements of merit to be taken into account in the promotion of employees and the appointment of candidates to positions in the public sector.
In the second paragraph it is stated that knowledge of both official languages is a pre-requisite for appointment to bilingual positions only, and that unilingual candidates who have in the prescribed manner expressed a willingness to become bilingual may participate in competitions for appointments to bilingual positions.
On the other hand, according to paragraph 3, where a position requires knowledge of one of the official languages, and not of the other, only candidates having an adequate knowledge of the required language may participate in the competition. Again, Mr. Speaker, these provisions do not really change the official languages policy. This fact is already recognized in another legislation, namely the Public Service Employment Act.
Section 10 of the Act states that appointments to or from within the Public Service shall be based on selection according to merit, as required by the Public Service Commission. This is a reassertion of the merit principle, a golden rule of the Commission. Under Section 12(1) of the same Act, which is related to section 10, the Commission may, in determining the basis of assessment of merit in relation to any position or class of positions, prescribe selection standards as the education, knowledge, experience, language, age, residence or any other matters that, in the opinion of the Commission, are necessary or desirable, considering the nature of duties to be performed. As for Section 20, it states that those employees appointed to serve in any department, or other portion of the Public Service, or part thereof, shall be qualified in the knowledge and use of the English or French language or both to the extent that the Commission deems necessary.
In addition, under section 30 of the Public Service Employment Act, where the Commission decides that it is not prati-cable nor in the best interests of the Public Service, it may, with the approval of the Governor in Council, exclude such

April 13, 1983
Official Languages Act
person or class of positions or persons from the operation of the present legislation. This gives some flexibility about which, in my opinion, English-speaking or French-speaking people cannot complain.
Under section 35 of the Public Service Employment Act, the Governor in Council, on the recommendation of the Commission, may make regulations prescribing how these persons excluded under section 39 shall be dealt with. When it comes to staffing bilingual positions, imperative or non-imperative, some sections of the Public Service Employment Act apply in a particular way.
It is interesting to note that the only element of our policy which was retained in Subsection 35.2 (2) of the Bill is the provision concerning what is usually called in bureaucratic circles non-imperative appointments. This provision has applied from the beginning of the linguistic reform and allows all unilingual candidates to apply for bilingual positions if they express the willingness to become bilingual and are able to do so within a given period.
Temporary, and in certain cases, permanent suspension of the merit principle is made possible by Section 39 of the Public Service Employment Act. The resulting exclusion order, which suspends application of Section 10 of the Public Service Employment Act, already provides that, in all cases where bilingual positions must be filled on a non-imperative basis, unilingual and bilingual candidates are eligible and can be considered on an equal footing as far as their linguistic qualifications are concerned. This exclusion applies to people whose candidacy for a bilingual position is considered for an unspecified period.
Mr. Speaker, all this shows that the new paragraph 2 included in the bill adds nothing new to the official languages policy. Moreover, it does not take into account imperative staffing which requires in certain cases, where there is a need for specialized knowledge or techniques or where certain operational necessities exist, for instance, that the linguistic requirements of a given bilingual position be met completely at the time of the appointment.
Mr. Speaker, it has in fact been said that if the proposed paragraph 2 were accepted and included in the Official Languages Act, it would mean a delay of several years in the official languages program as it would deny various departments and agencies the right to bill certain bilingual positions, with candidates who are linguistically qualified at the time of their appointment, which would remove from the Official Languages policy one of the levers with which the government has been able to hasten the pace of linguistic reform, especially in the area of services to the public.
In a few words, and I shall close with this comment, there is no need to reaffirm in the Official Languages Act something that already exists in the Public Service Act and the exclusion order on Official Languages in the Public Service. There must not be any confusion among responsibilities and jurisdictions. I believe that the flexibility of the Official Languages Act gives
everyone of both official languages equal chances to apply for positions and I do not believe that there can be any suspicion of discrimination in 1983.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING JOB OPPORTUNITIES FOR CERTAIN UNILINGUAL PUBLIC SERVICE EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
Madam Speaker, when introducing his Bill, the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine (Mr. McKenzie), in explaining what he had in mind, suggested that he was trying to amend the Official Languages Act to make it more clear that the merit principle for those entering the Public Service and those in it should be made much more explicit. The Hon. Member is considered by many people in the city which I represent as being opposed to the whole concept of bilingualism. I say to the Hon. Member that if he is, if that impression is correct, then he is in the minority, not just among Canadians but, indeed, in his Party as well.
Because the Hon. Member suggested that much of what was being done was never approved by Members of Parliament, I want to put on the record a couple of paragraphs from a speech made by the then Leader of the Conservative Party in Parliament, Mr. Stanfield, when the Bill was being debated. The speech was made on May 16, 1969, and reference can be found on page 8790 of that year's Hansard. On that occasion, Mr. Stanfield said:
This bill is placed before the House to strengthen rather than weaken Canadian unity. It is put forward for the purpose of making Canadians, whether they speak English or French, feel at home in this country to the extent that this is practical, and making federal government services available in the two languages. This was the principle which was discussed at the resolution stage. It was warmly accepted by all parties, including the New Democrats and Credi-tistes. Our task now is to judge the bill in the terms of these general purposes.
In the next passage, a translation from the French language, he said:
The purpose of this bill is not to compel English-speaking Canadians to learn French, and vice-versa. This bill is aimed at providing French-speaking or English-speaking minorities with all federal government services in the language of their choice, as far as it is practical.
Mr. Stanfield went on to support the Bill in principle, and a substantial majority of Conservative Members of Parliament voted for the Bill at that time, so I believe did all Members of our Party, all Members of the Creditiste Party, and all Members of the Liberal Party.
I understand the concerns of many people in this country. I represent a very ethnic constituency in which a majority of the people are of neither English nor French origin. My father came to this country from the Ukraine almost 80 years ago. I represent people of all races, religions and colours. It would take me nearly all my allotted time to simply list the various groups of people I represent. There are Ukrainians, Poles, Jews, Anglo-Saxons, Yugoslavs, Greeks, and I could go on and on. They worry about this bilingual policy, and I can understand it. They worry that somehow this Bill and what the Government has done in recent years makes them second-class citizens. That is not true.
April 13, 1983

This is a very large country geographically, and it has a pretty small population. As I have said, the people have come from all the continents. They are of different races, different colours and different religions.
The first Prime Minister of this country, Sir John A. MacDonald, helped set up the railway company, building the CPR from the Atlantic to the Pacific. Some of us may question the way in which he did it, and some of us may think that he gave away too much in order to do it. However, if that railway had not been built, there would not now be a country of Canada, because the economic lines on this continent run north and south rather than east and west. In a similar way, in the 1970s and through the 1980s, we have had to face up to the fact that the first language of almost a third of the people of this country is French. Eighty per cent of the people of Quebec are French-speaking. Close to 45 per cent of the people in New Brunswick are French.
