speechtext: No, 38 per cent.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT RESPECTING JOB OPPORTUNITIES FOR CERTAIN UNILINGUAL PUBLIC SERVICE EMPLOYEES
speechtext:
I stand corrected by the Hon. Member who comes from New Brunswick. Almost 40 per cent of the people in New Brunswick are French-speaking. Their forefathers were here before Canada was a country. They very strongly believe that they have a right to be served in their language- French-when they have dealings with the federal Government, with any Department or agency of the Government; just as English-speaking people, for example, in a city like Quebec City, feel that they have a right to deal with the federal Government or any of its Departments or agencies in the English language. That is precisely what Mr. Stanfield, who was then Leader of the Conservative Party, said in the part of his speech which I quoted. That is what the Official Languages Act spells out, and that is what Members of Parliament, by an overwhelming majority, supported when the Bill was before Parliament and when it was enacted.
Does that mean that Members of Parliament, whatever Party they come from, agree with everything which the Government has done to implement the Official Languages Act? Of course not, Mr. Speaker. However, I say to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine that a vast majority of the people of Canada understand the reasons we have adopted and supported this kind of policy. All the polls prove that. I do not have the time today, but when I spoke during the debate on this Bill in 1969, I placed on the record the results of polls which were taken across Canada at that time, and I could do it again if anyone is interested.
I say to the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine that he should realistically look at what is happening in our own city in which the percentage of French-speaking people is relatively small. An increasing number of young people are being urged by their parents to attend French immersion schools. I have a six year old grand-daughter who attends a French immersion school. The complaints in Winnipeg are not that we have too many French immersion classes but, rather, that we do not have enough. I do not think there is one Hon. Member from Winnipeg who can deny that.
Official Languages Act
The Manitoba Government has gone a step further. It has said to the people of Manitoba that where an appreciable number of people who are of neither English-speaking nor French-speaking origin want to have a good part of their children's schooling conducted in another language, they can have it. Therefore, classes in the public school system are conducted not only in English and French, but also speaking from memory, in German, in Polish and in Hebrew, and that program is being extended.
The French immersion program is growing by leaps and bounds every year. The only thing which holds it back from growing even faster than it has is financial constraint. I will deal with that topic in a few moments.
OO)
I want to make it clear that it has never been suggested that every public servant must be bilingual. However, I have received some complaints and have dealt with individual cases where I thought a Department was implementing the policy wrongly. After all, we must recognize that in much of Canada where about 95 per cent of the people speak English, few French-speaking public servants are needed to deal with them in French. Similarly, in many parts of French Canada where there are a small number of English-speaking Canadians, few English-speaking public servants are required to deal with those Canadians in the English language.
While I do not agree with every decision that has been made by various Departments, the basic principle of bilingualism is one that the vast majority of Members of Parliament supported when it was implemented in 1969. I am sure that Hon. Members still support that principle.
The Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine quoted certain Government documents which specifically refer to encouraging francophones to come into a certain branch of the Public Service. To understand the real situation we would have to consider individual cases, not just in a few minutes in the House but in a committee where these cases can be studied in depth. The fact of the matter is that the Canadian Public Service has had far fewer francophone public servants in proportion to the number of French Canadians. When I was studying this question in 1969 there was a report which indicated that among the 1,100 senior public servants, just over 10 per cent were francophones. When this is compared to the 30 per cent francophone population, it is evident that we have never been overstaffed with francophone public servants. Despite the fact that this percentage is probably higher today than it was in 1969, I am certain that it is still far from 30 per cent.
I am not suggesting that quotas should be put in place. I am simply saying that when one looks at the issue realistically, the percentage of anglophone public servants at this time is still much higher in proportion to the anglophone population.
I wish to say to the Hon. Member that I can understand the Public Service making a special effort to hire more francophones, and I wish it would make a similar effort to include more natives in the Public Service. In order to accomplish this

April 13, 1983
Canada Labour Code
we must change our old concepts about merit. While merit is an important factor when hiring and people should have the education and training that is needed for a particular job opening, if we adhere to the old ideas and very technical requirements of job merit, it will be generations before native people, for example, will enter the Public Service in any kind of appreciable numbers.
I hope the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine will consider this in the days to come: unless we make special efforts to persuade and recruit more native people into the federal and provincial Public Service as well as private sector jobs, they will remain among the poorest, least educated, least healthy, highest unemployed and worst housed in the country.
It is necessary for us to develop new concepts and consider affirmative action in order to deal with this problem. 1 am not opposed to federal Government Departments making special efforts to recruit francophones in areas where there have been very few of them or none at all. While merit is still an important consideration, in order to achieve our collective goal of uniting the country we must face reality and include people in the Public Service from all the groups which make up this country.
I previously indicated that I have occasionally felt a mistake was made in individual cases respecting bilingualism. The hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine, and I am sure many other Members, have heard of individual cases where people have felt they were unfairly treated because of this program, or perhaps some other program. When I have felt a mistake was made, I have taken it up with the Government Department concerned-sometimes successfully and sometimes unsuccessfully.
When we say that we support bilingualism in the Public Service, we are indicating our belief in the principle that the Public Service should be made more accessible and capable of dealing with Canadians in the language of their choice. While this policy specifically concerns English and French, there are many newcomers to this country who speak neither French nor English. It is important that they be able to deal with a Government Department or agency. Therefore, there should be people in the Public Service who speak the languages of our recent immigrants.
In conclusion, let me reiterate what I said in the beginning and what I have tried to say whenever this question has been debated in the House and elsewhere: that I and my Party support the principle of bilingualism which is the cornerstone of the Official Languages Act. We voted for it when it was introduced, as did the majority from every Party, including the Progressive Conservatives at that time. While we still believe that it is the proper policy, it is probably quite true that mistakes have been made. For example, I suggest that the program to train thousands of public servants to speak a second language, which was a major expense and effort, was a failure to a large extent and probably a mistake when it was conceived. Most of those people were unable to learn a second language sufficiently to be able to put it to practical use. A few
of those who did learn the second language use it very infrequently. I believe that the money and effort would have been much better spent in educating young people and promoting a second language at the learning stage. There are ordinary citizens in Holland, Belgium, Norway and Germany who speak up to three and four languages. It is only arrogance on the part of the English-speaking people to believe that everybody else should learn their language while they do not have to learn any other language.
Therefore, we support the idea of bilingualism which is enshrined in the Bill. We support the programs which have encouraged young people and other Canadians to learn a second language. While this Bill is fundamentally good, we believe it should be reviewed. The way bilingualism is being implemented, it should be carefully studied because mistakes have been made and should be corrected. I do not believe that this amendment adds anything to the objectives which we already have.

speakeroldname: Mr. Lyle S. Kristiansen (Kootenay West) moved
speechtext:
that Bill C-557, an Act to amend the Canada Labour Code (unjust dismissal), be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration.
He said: Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak to Bill C-557 I would like to say at the outset that the principle of the Bill is very simple and can be stated very briefly. It is simply that workers should not be fired for obeying the law. Conversely, what this Bill would do, if implemented, is to prevent an employee from being fired or otherwise disciplined by his employer for refusing to obey a direct order from his employer if he reasonably believed that if he were to follow such an
April 13, 1983

order his action would place him, the employee, in violation of any law or statute.
I think it goes almost without saying that the principle underlying the Bill itself is a reasonable one. It is a principle enshrined with regard to occupational health and safety legislation in many jurisdictions across Canada. It is one in which we have been engaged in discussions with the federal Government over the last three or four years in order to have the principle enshrined more appropriately within Part IV of the Canada Labour Code. This Bill goes much further than attempting to protect the right to health and safety of employees across this country.
That is not the kind of issue that initially gave rise to my particular concern with the need for such legislation. In fact my motivation stemmed from an incident that took place in the Queen Charlotte Islands, B.C. when sixteen loggers were arrested because they were ordered by their employer to cut an area that had been declared off-limits to logging by federal fisheries officials. Many of us felt the order of the federal Government was quite appropriate. It had followed a considerable degree of investigation and there had been considerable disagreement with the provincial Forestry Department in B.C. at that time. Irrespective of whether that initial decision not to log that area was correct, what was done was totally unfair. I and many others in British Columbia and I think across the country who were aware of the incident felt it was totally unfair to arrest and jail 16 employees of a particular logging company because they had followed the very clear and specific orders of their employer. The employer thought he was obeying the law as interpreted by the Government of British Columbia. He realized he was in some disagreement with the federal authority.
In order to allow employees to assist in the enforcement of law, I and a number of others feel it is rather important, not just for the sake of occupational health and safety, not just for health matters in a broader spirit, not just relating to matters of the environment or to matters of fisheries, that we should attempt to enlist the assistance of working people, men and women across the country, in standing up for the laws which we have enacted in our wisdom, in either the federal Parliament, the provincial Parliaments or elsewhere, and in the enactment of a law to protect society as a whole or particular sectors of it. It is unrealistic to expect a working person, particularly in economic times like these which are not so different from situations in certain industries even going back to 1979, to risk his or her livelihood and perhaps even the existence of families. We know what happens to families which go for extended periods in these times without a source of income. It is unfair to expect them to put themselves at risk and put their jobs, their livelihoods at risk, unless there is some protection for them.
The incident at Riley Creek which took place in the early months of 1979 again followed the enactment by Parliament in 1978 of a law to protect fish breeding and spawning rivers. Federal Fisheries officers had to arrest loggers when their
Canada Labour Code
cutting operations threatened Riley Creek, an important salmon ground in the Queen Charlotte Islands. Eight employees were arrested initially and a further eight later. Following long discussion and arguments between federal and provincial Governments, finally a stay of proceedings was instituted, but the lesson was quite clear.
Surely it is preferable in the enforcement of legislation, whether environmental or in dealing with health and safety, to have on the spot enforcement by citizens. If that can be done in a peaceful and legitimate manner it is preferable than having to hire additional large numbers of inspection and enforcement officers from either federal or provincial jurisdictions. In fact, the history of enforcement of many of our laws is a very sad one. We have many, many statutes on the books across Canada, federal and provincial, in which we either did not put enforcement mechanisms into play or, for financial, budgetary or other reasons, do not provide the wherewithal for hiring inspection and enforcement officers or for hiring sufficient numbers of them to attempt to ensure that the laws we have in place are observed. It is not enough to assume, as some idealistic people sometimes do, that because we pass a law it actually changes anything. There are too many motivations which cause people to act in other ways. We are all aware of those.
I have one example and although it comes under provincial jurisdiction, it is not exactly typical, but it is a glaring example of what can happen. In the Province of British Columbia for many years we have had an Act called the Factories Act which was passed in the 1920s or 1930s. In the late 1960s many of us in my corner of B.C. became aware for the first time, that there was such a piece of legislation. We phoned the provincial Department of Labour. We could not find anyone in any Department who said the Bill came within the responsibility of their Ministry or Department. Most people, even in the Department of Labour which was finally found to be responsible, did not even know of its existence. The Factories Act provided for health, working conditions legislation, heat and appropriate light in virtually thousands of industrial installations across the Province.
When the New Democratic Party administration of Dave Barrett was elected in 1972, we found that there were two inspectors, not only to enforce that body of legislation but to carry on the inspection required by law to ensure that any new industrial installation would comply with the laws and regulations as well. When we asked them how they did their job, we were told "telephon book inspections". At that time I asked them what they meant. I asked whether they telephoned the thousands of companies on the list, just the two of them, to see whether they were in compliance with the law. I asked, "Did you just ask them that question?" They said, "No, we did not have time to do that. We just copied the names of the companies out of the telephone book and into our records to show that we had considered them."

April 13, 1983
Canada Labour Code
When it came to the working conditions of thousands of British Columbians in industrial installations, that was the kind of enforcement there was of the law which the legislature of that Province in its wisdom had decided to place on the books, presumably with some debate, some decades before.
I am not suggesting that we are sinning quite to that extent. A number of my colleagues and I took tours across Canada related to what we hope are still forthcoming amendments to the Canada Labour Code. We have been told that these amendments were coming since we were first elected in 1980. We visited many parts of the country. For instance, on the waterfront of Saint John, New Brunswick, there were only one or two federal officers presumably available to consider any breaches of health and safety regulations relating to the transport industry and the docks in that entire area. They also had many other duties which took them outside the immediate vicinity of Saint John. If we want some enforcement of the laws on the books, whether it is to protect the environment and, with the increasing exploration, presumably the development of many energy resources in the far North of Canada, surely it is important to have as much self-enforcement by the people working in those industries as possible. There is no way the Government, or almost any Government, could conceivably have enough people present throughout the Arctic or in the Canadian offshore to ensure that either environmental laws or health and safety laws are enforced.
We can all say that working people, like companies, ought to do their jobs, obey the law and do the right thing, even if they put themselves, their incomes or profits at risk. We know that people do not normally do that, so the least we can do is to provide some security of employment for those who, of their own volition, decide that they should stand up and attempt to enforce the laws of the land simply by refusing to pursue tasks which they know or reasonably believe to be in violation of the laws.
I hope Government representatives will seriously consider such legislation; whether or not it is in this exact form, certainly the thrust of it. Also I hope for the support of Hon. Members of the Official Opposition. I would be agreeable to withdrawing the Bill if there were agreement that the subject matter of it be referred to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration. We hope that that Committee will soon have an opportunity to consider the amendments to Parts III, IV and V of the Canada Labour Code, which we have been assured were coming for some years now. At the same time it would be appropriate, as Members from all sides are attempting to draw up a more reasonable definition of the right of employees to refuse to obey an order when their lives are placed in jeopardy, to realize that it is the right of Canadian employees to stand up in good conscience and say that they will not do work which violates the laws of the land as passed by the House of Commons or other legislatures across the country. I think that plea is clear and fair. I hope for the cooperation of Hon. Members opposite on this occasion, but if not at this time, hopefully at some time soon in the future.
Perhaps they would consent to the kind of request I have included in my remarks.
The principle that workers should not be fired for obeying the laws is self-evident. I hope other Hon. Members will see the issue likewise.

speakeroldname: Mr. Andre Maltais (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce and Minister of Regional Economic Expansion):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Regional Economic Expansion; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I greatly appreciated the comments made by the Member opposite concerning the problem of worker safety, in connection with improvements to our labour laws which have now made it possible for workers to work safely without constraints that might engender problems of a physical nature or unfair working conditions, as a result of doing work that infringes, legislation that provides for the worker's right to job security and job safety.
Mr. Speaker, I am particularly pleased to be speaking to this Bill because I represent a riding where 85 per cent of the workers are unionized and employed in the private sector. Baie-Comeau, Port-Cartier, Sept-Iles, Schefferville, Gagnon and Fermont-everywhere I go I meet workers, and I believe I am very aware of the problems raised earlier by the Member opposite. I feel it is absolutely essential to have strong labour relations and just and fair laws that provide maximum safety for workers, because profits, production and a good labour force are also the result of laws that provide for a safe job environment.
On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, the Bill before the House today, Bill C-557, seems a little unclear in parts, because the Canada Labour Code already contains sections that are abundantly clear and already provide, practically word for word, the same elements as Bill C-557. For instance, in Section 184, it says quite clearly . . . But first I would like to quote from Bill C-557, which stipulates the following:
No employer and no person acting on behalf of an employer shall suspend, discharge, or impose any financial or other penalty on an employee, or take any other disciplinary action against an employee, by reason of his refusal to perform an act that he has reasonable cause to believe is prohibited by law.
The Canada Labour Code, Part IV, Industrial Relations, contains the following provisions regarding unfair dismissal and unfair practice, and if you compare both paragraphs, they are very similar. I refer to section 184.3, and I quote:
(3) No employer and no person acting on behalf of an employer shall (c) suspend, discharge or impose any financial or other penalty on an employee, or take any other disciplinary action against an employee, by reason of his refusal to perform all or some of the duties and responsibilities of another employee who is participating in a strike that is not prohibited by this Part;
(0 suspend, discharge or impose any financial or other penalty on a person employed by him, or take any other disciplinary action against such a person, by reason of that person having refused to perform an act prohibited by this Part;
Both these paragraphs deal with the right of an employee to refuse to take part in activities which he thinks may be contrary to the Canada Labour Code, as well as with the rights of employees who take part in a legal strike.
April 13, 1983

For all practical purposes, these provisions provide employees with protection against any disciplinary action an employer might take against them in violation of the Labour Code. This would apply to a strike situation, but it is going even further, for the Canada Labour Code is quite clear in two other sections which resemble closely those which appear in the bill introduced by the Hon. Member.
Mr. Speaker, Part IV of the Canada Labour Code deals with health, safety and protection of employees, and I think these are major items. It is very similar to what the Hon. Member is seeking through his bill. Section 81(1) of the Canada Labour Code states, and I quote:
81.(1) Every person operating or carrying on a federal work, undertaking or business shall do so in a manner that will not endanger the safety or health of any person employed thereupon or in connection therewith.
Then, there is Section 82.1 which states, and I quote:
Where a person employed upon or in connection with the operation of any federal work, undertaking or business has reasonable cause to believe that
(a)	the use or operation of a machine, device or thing would constitute an
imminent danger to the safety or health of himself or another employee, or
(b)	a condition exists in any place that would constitute an imminent danger to
his own safety or health,
that person may refuse to use or operate the machine, device or thing or to work in the place.
Mr. Speaker, I feel that we are really coming to the heart of the matter which the hon. member has raised, because the Canada Labour Code is clearly protecting employees both in strike and health or safety situations, when it states that an employee may refuse to use or operate a machine, device or thing or to work in the place.
Earlier, the Hon. Member gave an example of an incident he had witnessed in his riding, something to do with a forest worker who had experienced a problem because there were some factors which-it would seem, in light of the Hon. Member's remarks-did put his health or safety in jeopardy. I am surprised that anything like that might have occurred because the fact is that the Canada Labour Code is very clear about workers' rights. In that respect, I suggest that a reference to the sections I have just read would be ample proof.
And that is not all. It is clearly stated that, judging from the quotations given and related to Parts III, IV and V of the Canada Labour Code, any employee who is wronged, whether or not he belongs to a union and is protected by a collective agreement, has the option to launch an appeal in the case of unwarranted dismissal resulting from an order which itself calls for a violation of the Code. As to other laws, the Criminal Code also provides appeal opportunities for any employee forced to break the law by his employer.
In short, the Bill recommends close supervision of the application of the Canada Labour Code provisions relating to security and safety in the work place. Yet, I do not see what Bill C-557 adds at this time, because if you look at chapters 3, 4 and 5 of the Code, those aspects are very well defined. On the other hand, the Member raised a point about inspectors which is worth paying attention to. In my region for example, in my constituency of Manicouagan which I visit quite regularly, I meet a lot of union members. As I mentioned previously,
Canada Labour Code
85 percent of all workers in that area are union members. It is important to go and check whether the assessment of their work place or their working conditions by workers is well founded or true to reality. One often has to turn to the inspector, but according to all current collective agreements, if the worker is a member of a union, he can file a grievance. This is the usual method used by unions in order to correct problems relating to the application of collective agreements since current agreements cover quite obviously all the specific issues raised by the Hon. Member.
That explains why I have difficulty in seeing the advantages of the Bill proposed by the Member. We may be able later on to discuss it during the question and answer period, but on the basis of the earlier presentation by the Member, I have difficulty in seeing anything that is not already in the Canada Labour Code.
As far as inspectors are concerned, I believe that each company, each union and each employee should know the various possible recourses in cases of abuse where an employer or a foreman assigns a worker to operations in an environment that seems unsafe, and the same goes with respect to equipment or work site. But with reference to the Bill introduced by the Hon. Member, after I have read the proposal, it is my view that additions could hardly be made. I have here in my hand this Bill in which it is provided, and I quote:
The Canada Labour Code is amended by adding, immediately after section 184 thereof, the following section:
184.1 No employer and no person acting on behalf of an employer shall suspend, discharge, or impose any financial or other penalty on an employee, or take any other disciplinary action against an employee, by reason of his refusal to perform an act that he has reasonable cause to believe is prohibited by law.
Madam Speaker, this is exactly what is said in the Canadian Labour Code. And this would call for further clarification. If the aim is to protect the worker, such protection is afforded by collective bargaining. He is also protected by the Canadian Labour Code so clearly the worker is amply protected in that area.
But what I find amazing in the Hon. Member's proposal is that in my own constituency, I never had any workers coming to me and complaining that they were not adequately protected. If ever there was a lact of protection, it could have been at the Iron Ore Company where everyone was laid off, but then that is another kind of protection. It may be a matter for discussion with the next leader of the Progressive Conservative Party. The protection workers are now looking for is job security in my view, not the addition of new sections to the Canadian Labour Code. At any rate, I would like to discuss the matter with the Hon. Member, because when I read his Bill, there is something I find hard to grasp, because it seems to me that these are aspects that are already provided for in the Canadian Labour Code.
The other point that it would perhaps be interesting to raise at this time, Mr. Speaker, is how the Departments inspect the various worksites. I believe that it would be possible to improve the inspection mechanism. However, inspectors go out to the

April 13, 1983
Canada Labour Code
worksites to see what is going on quite regularly and there are therefore direct and regular contacts between the unions and the provincial and federal Labour Departments to determine what improvements could be made on either side. As far as I know, most often, management attends these meetings to see what can be done to improve the welfare of its workers. This occurs on a normal and regular basis in all businesses, whether big or medium-size. Even in the case of smaller businesses, provincial regulations provide normal and well-protected conditions for the workers.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, abuses are always possible. It is quite obvious that every eventuality cannot be foreseen. Two years ago, for instance, an underground gallery of the Noranda mine in the Abitibi region caved in and it was left up to the court to determine who was responsible, but the inspections had been carried out normally and the union inspectors had done their job. However, there can be unforeseen circumstances or cases of negligence. This cannot be denied. No statute can provide for every situation and it would certainly be unrealistic to think that every case can be foreseen and provided for in detail in the Canada Labour Code. This is quite unthinkable. However, to improve the situation, there is nothing to prevent the Hon. Member from making representations to the Standing Committee on Labour, Manpower and Immigration, perhaps to have additional regulations established. This would be a good thing. On this side of the House, we would be quite willing to consider new elements which could truly apply to the Canada Labour Code. However, I believe that a Bill designed to integrate the proposals of the Hon. Member into the Canada Labour Code would add nothing useful for the moment.
Perhaps it would be more interesting for a Standing Committee of the House to consider what can be done as regards regulations because in the Canada Labour Code itself the parameters are well delineated. It would be useless to amend the Code without providing further protection, because that is important. It is not enough to amend the Labour Code. We should really try to provide the worker with better protection.
If we look at the Canada Labour Code, as I said earlier, we will note that already there are provisions stating that an employee may refuse to perform work that he believes to be unlawful and the legislation sets forth certain procedures which must be followed. It would perhaps be advisable to give a few examples. There is the case of an employee who refuses to do some work because he believes it is prejudicial to his health. This is in a way the issue raised by the Hon. Member a short while ago. Now any employee who follows the correct procedure but who is fired by his employer for having exercised his right to refuse to work may lodge an appeal with the Canada Labour Relations Board. There definitely exists an appeal procedure, representative of the working world, the main task of which is to judge and interpret these circumstances. Naturally, if the employee has not followed the rules, the Canada Labour Relations Board will be unable to hear his claim; he could, however, refer to the provisions concerning
unjust dismissal contained in Part III of the Canadian Labour Code, under Division V.7.
I would also like, Mr. Speaker, to remind the House that the amendments to the Labour Code that were passed on September 1, 1978, allow an employee who believes he has been unjustly dismissed to bring an appeal if his employer is subject to the Code. Except, of course, that the employee has to prove that there was imminent danger. If I interpret correctly the provisions of Bill C-557, the question of impending danger is there, and if not, perhaps the Member could rectify later. I take it for granted that the Member wishes with his Bill to focus on the health and security aspects in the work place itself as well as on the methods or the equipment used.
That piece of legislation provided for security of employment for a larger number of people since it gave non-union employees unjustly dismissed the opportunity to get their job back, whereas before only union members could do that through collective bargaining. Indeed, when an employee is dismissed because he refused to work when he felt that his health was placed in jeopardy or something else, he can apply to the Canada Labour Relations Board, and if his grievance is really well-founded, then the Board is empowered to reinstate in his job the employee found unjustly dismissed. I believe that shows very clearly that there is some security of employment, and that responsibilities must be established by a third party which is neutral with regard to the case in dispute.
So on that point, Mr. Speaker, I think there is already some protection for the employee. There is no doubt that the sponsor of Bill C-557 is convinced that with these amendments employees will be even more able to refuse to do work they believe to be in violation of the law. I am sure no Member of this House, whatever his or her political affiliation, would be against legislation aimed at improving the situation. I suggest all of us want to improve labour conditions, to insure that people who work in a given sector can enjoy as much security as is possible. However, the bill being considered does not contain anything new, as I was saying, and that is where my problem is. That is where lies the difficulty we see, on this side of the House. Really, this bill does not bring forward anything new, whether we consider it from the point of view of law or from the point of view of security at work. That is my problem. As we have seen, under Parts III, IV and V of the Canada Labour Code that were quoted earlier, an employee, even if he is not a member of a union and is not protected by a collective agreement, has many possibilities under the Canada Labour Code to seek redress when he feels he has been unjustly fired after having been ordered to commit an act which would constitute a violation to the Canada Labour Code.
So, Mr. Speaker, I would like to emphasize this: the worker remains free to judge by himself of the security offered either by the company he works for, by the machinery or by the work place, and he remains free to refuse to work. Then, if he is fired for having done so, he submits his case to the Canada Labour Board. The case is reviewed by a third party and justice is done according to an assessment. I believe this
April 13, 1983

process does respect individual freedom and insure that justice is done.
For all these reasons, Mr. Speaker, and 1 will come to the point since my time is expired, 1 believe that at this stage, the reasons put forward by the Hon. Member are not sufficient ground and it would be difficult for me or for Members on this side of the House to bring our support to this bill. However, we would be most happy, Mr. Speaker, to receive advice pertaining to eventual amendments which would bring about something new. But for the time being, I suggest this bill does not propose anything new and would not provide more security for the worker.
Mr. Speaker, I do not know if the Hon. Member has time left and would accept a question.

Mr. Speaker, it struck me that the Hon. Member misunderstood the intent of the Bill. I would ask him to read Clause 184.1 again and see whether he would not agree that the intent is to protect broadly the right of an employee to refuse to commit an act that touched on matters outside his or her personal security, and is not meant to have the narrower intent whether a strike is in process or his own life or safety or that of other employees may be affected.
Would the Hon. Member not agree that the purpose of the Bill is to allow an employee, by refusing, to enforce other laws, for instance, affecting the security of the fishing industry or other elements of the population or hazards as a result of transportation regulations or environmental regulations such as the disposition of mine tailings or air and water pollutants? There are other actions which cannot be covered specifically in the law. Would the Hon. Member not agree that there is an argument to be made for legislation that would allow employees to enforce that other body of law, rather than society having to hire an army of inspectors to enforce each and every item?

Mr. Speaker, first of all, 1 want to congratulate the Hon. Member for his dedication to the well-being of the workers. His concern is most legitimate and commendable, but I would like to remind him that fishermen are normally considered self-employed because they frequently own their boat and they carry personal insurance. If they are members of a fishing crew, they are covered by group insurance. Here is an example that the House may find amusing. A large part of the coast of Manicouagan is inhabited by fishermen. You know very well, Mr. Speaker, the conditions these people have to live in. If you go to sea and there is a storm, there is nothing to protect you because you are 10, 20 or 200 miles away in waters
Canada Labour Code
now under Canadian jurisdiction, and anything can happen. Fishermen on a ship owned by a company are frequently covered by group insurance. The ship is insured. But the captain must try to bring the ship back to port as fast as possible for protection. It is not through legislation that we are going to prevent storms.
There is also a second element. We were talking about fishermen and I think it is a good example. A clear difference must be made between the self-employed fisherman and the fisherman working for a company. Let us speak about personal and collective insurance. Fishermen are now covered by collective agreements and, in certain cases, by the Canada Labour Code, just like people working on a farm, in a pulp and paper mill, in a processing plant or a factory.
Therefore, I concur with the Hon. Member about the need for protection in some areas. There are certainly cases that have been overlooked and which must be reorganized, but when we speak of air quality and pretend that it is necessary to make sure that these people are not in danger, maybe we should apply the provisions of the Canadian Labour Code to fishermen working on a lake contaminated by acid rains. For example, in case of rain, everybody would have to go home because there is imminent danger. Therefore, it would be necessary to decide what that is and I think that many factors would have to be taken into consideration. So, I assume that the concern of the Hon. Member is sincere, but as far as the application is concerned, it is not legislation at this stage which will permit to improve things, but that would probably merit further attention. I gave examples, Mr. Speaker, which may seem extreme to some Hon. Members, but if we were only a little bit closer to fishermen, we would see that my examples for the fishing industry are real. Earlier, the Hon. Member mentioned healthy working conditions. I find it difficult to include this in legislation.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak to Bill C-557, an Act to amend the Canada Labour Code. This is a Private Member's Bill put forth by the Hon. Member for Kootenay West (Mr. Kristiansen), and it had its first reading on May 2, 1980. This Bill would not, I am convinced, provide any additional protection for workers other than that which already exists under Parts III, IV and V of the Canada Labour Code and the Criminal Code of Canada.
The underlying principle of the existing provisions of the Canada Labour Code is that "Termination of employment should not take place unless there is a valid reason for such termination connected with the capacity or conduct of the worker or based on the operational requirements of the undertaking, establishment or service." The amendments made in 1978 to the Canada Labour Code which effectively protect workers from unjust dismissals, were a result of a struggle and

April 13, 1983
Canada Labour Code
reaction against the authoritarianism of employers of a past age.
It is interesting to note, Mr. Speaker, that these amendments afford aggrieved workers safeguards against dismissal which fall in line with procedures for enabling workers to contest arbitrary dismissal, either by law or in voluntary collective agreements which exist in Belgium, France, The Federal Republic of Germany, Italy, Luxembourg, Netherlands, the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Northern Ireland. Canada, together with other western industrialized nations, recognizes that the concept of giving workers a greater sense of security is an important step to improving industrial relations. Dismissal is no longer considered solely a matter for decision by the employer. I believe it is true to say, Mr. Speaker, that most people in industry today recognize that workers need to have proper safeguards against unjust dismissal. Great strides have been made in recent years in strengthening workers' rights and status in their employment. Employers and the labour movement alike realize that fair and sensible procedures, clearly established and understood by workers and management at all levels, can do much to improve industrial relations by preventing grievances and disputes over dismissals. The provisions existing in the Canada Labour Code allow workers who feel they have been unjustly dismissed to have ample recourse to contest the action.
The Bill presently before this House, Mr. Speaker, I would respectfully suggest, does not add in any way additional protection for workers who have been unjustly dismissed. Neither does the proposed amendment promote an increased sense of security for employees. 1 would direct your attention, Mr. Speaker, to the fact that worker discipline may take many forms. However, it generally falls into three categories. There are warnings, suspensions and dismissals. Although Part III of the Canada Labour Code is concerned only with dismissals, it should be recognized that they may be preceded by some form of progressive disciplinary action, which includes at least two written warnings, followed by suspension, which in turn is followed by dismissal. The degree of progressive discipline usually relates to the severity of the misconduct by the employee, that is, outright dismissal may occur if the misconduct is extremely serious.
In any disciplinary situation there may be mitigating factors. When an employer decides to dismiss an employee he should thoroughly investigate the matter to ensure that all mitigating factors have been carefully considered. This is not
only good business practice, it is simply common sense. Arbitration decisions have resulted in a list of factors which ought to be taken into consideration when faced with this issue.
Further, I believe that it is important that employees be made fully aware of the standards of conduct to which they are expected to adhere. The rules should be readily available, and the employer should take all possible steps to make sure employees know and understand them. It is the employer's burden to prove that dismissal was warranted. However, it is important to remember that both management and employees have specific responsibilities. Based on past performance, it is reasonable to assume that adjudicators dealing with appeals against dismissal will objectively judge each case on its own merits and decide whether the employer had just cause to dismiss the employee.
In light of the forgoing, Mr. Speaker, I would respectfully suggest that provisions now existing in the Canada Labour Code are designed to give employees ample recourse to redress a dismissal they judge to be wrongful, and further, that Bill C-557 should not succeed.
